item.title: Baidu released ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base
item.author: pretext
item.content:encoded:
A base model is valuable both for the capabilities that pre-training builds and for the starting point it offers for further training. Different domains, reasoning tasks and agentic applications call for different data, training objectives and behaviors. Releasing the weights at the end of pre-training lets developers build on the general capabilities already in place and choose for themselves where to take the model next.Today we are releasing , a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model with total parameters, of which are activated per token. It was pre-trained from scratch on with a training context of up to , and supports a context for fine-tuning and inference. The weights are the checkpoint at the end of pre-training, before any mid- or post-training, and can serve as a common starting point for domain adaptation, instruction tuning and reinforcement-learning research.To be worth building on, a base model has to stay affordable to train and run, so efficiency was a design goal from the outset. Further training samples from the model repeatedly, and agentic applications bring multi-turn interactions and long contexts. Both add to compute and memory costs. ERNIE 5.5 Flash therefore revisits the trade-off between capability and efficiency in every component, from attention and residual connections to the MoE layers and the output head, and weighs activated compute, KV cache and long-context cost together rather than one at a time.The same thinking shaped the data and the training system. Every later stage of training builds on what pre-training provides, so the corpus emphasizes capabilities that are hard to add afterwards, such as repository-scale code and long-context understanding. And because an efficient architecture pays off only if it can also be trained efficiently at scale, we designed the model and the training system together.We hope this release spares more developers the cost of large-scale pre-training, so they can spend their own resources on the capabilities, tasks and training methods they care about.An open starting point for further training. Base weights with no mid- or post-training, leaving the community free to pursue its own approaches to domain adaptation, reasoning and agent training.Built for efficient further training and inference. Sparse MoE and hybrid sparse attention balance model capacity, activated compute and long-context cost in the architecture itself.Broad data, efficient training. Diverse, high-quality pre-training data gives later training a well-rounded foundation, and a training system co-designed with the architecture keeps large-scale pre-training efficient.A clean research baseline. A single checkpoint taken at the end of pre-training makes it easy to compare training methods under controlled conditions and to measure what each one adds.ERNIE 5.5 Flash has 43 Transformer layers, a hidden size of 4096 and 64 attention heads.2.1 Latent-Gated Sparse AttentionHybrid MLA + HCA attention: Most layers need only a coarse view of the distant past, so only one layer in seven keeps token-level access to the full context, using Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA). The remaining layers use Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA): each compresses every 128 tokens into a single cached entry, then attends to all of these entries plus a short window of recent, uncompressed tokens. An HCA layer therefore still sees the whole sequence, while caching only a small fraction of what a full-context layer needs.Layer-specific head dimensions: Instead of using the same head dimension in every layer, we set it according to how expensive each layer's attention is: cheap layers get wide heads, expensive layers get narrower ones. HCA layers attend over a sequence compressed 128×, so their attention is cheap and they can afford wide 512-dim heads at little extra compute. MLA layers attend at token level and cost more, so they use narrower 256-dim heads for both query/key and value.Concentrating the KV-cache budget on MLA layers: With HCA in most layers, the main question is where to spend the rest of the KV-cache budget. One option is many Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) layers, which compress the history 4× and attend only to a selected part of it. We instead use a few MLA layers that keep every token. In our pre-training comparisons at a similar KV-cache budget, HCA combined with MLA outperforms HCA combined with CSA.Sparse attention in the full-context layers: The MLA layers are the only layers that see every distant token individually. With dense attention, they would account for most of the attention compute at long context lengths, so they use sparse attention (DSA) instead. A lightweight indexer scores past positions for each query, and core attention is computed only over the top-k highest-scoring positions. The per-query cost of core attention therefore stays constant as the context grows. With DSA, these layers match dense attention in pre-training loss and train substantially faster.Two further changes apply inside the attention layers:Low-Rank Gated Attention: Gated attention multiplies the attention output by a learned gate, which has been shown to improve both quality and training stability. Normally the gate is computed from the layer's hidden state. We instead compute it from the low-rank query latent, a compressed form of the query that each attention layer already computes. Because this latent is 4× narrower than the hidden state, the gate projection has 75% fewer weights, and our ablations also show better performance. Every attention layer in ERNIE 5.5 Flash, MLA and HCA alike, uses Low-Rank Gated Attention. After attention, VHA adds a lightweight low-rank mixing step across heads, with an identity skip connection. This lets heads share information, which improves expressiveness and training quality, and at inference it is fused into the attention kernel with negligible overhead.2.2 Multi-Router Latent MoEA conventional MoE layer picks experts with a single router and a hard top-k. We find that a single router's scores correlate only weakly with how useful each expert actually is, especially in the middle and deeper layers. And because experts left out of the top-k receive no gradient from that token, the router gets no signal that it chose wrongly, so wrong selections tend to reinforce themselves.Multi-Router replaces the single router with several independently initialized sigmoid routers that score the experts jointly. The routers develop clearly distinct preferences: an expert can be chosen because one router strongly favors it or because several favor it together, so a wrong choice is easier to correct. The errors of any one router no longer decide the selection, and routing becomes less sensitive to noisy features and distribution shift. The number of activated experts, expert FLOPs and communication volume stay the same. Compared with a single router, routing scores correlate noticeably better with how useful each expert is, with the largest gains in the middle and deeper layers.All layers except the first use an MoE feed-forward block:512 routed experts (top-10) plus 1 shared expert, with auxiliary-loss-free, bias-corrected load balancing. Each MoE layer first projects tokens from 4096 to a 2048-d latent space; the experts (intermediate size 2048) run in that space, and a single shared up-projection maps the result back to 4096. This roughly halves dispatch/combine traffic and expert FLOPs relative to full-width experts.Stable LatentMoE design with learnable scalars. The MoE blocks follow the Stable LatentMoE design (an RMSNorm before the up-projection and SiTU-GLU expert activations), which keeps expert outputs well scaled across all 43 layers and stabilizes optimization. In addition, each routed expert's routing weight is multiplied by its own learnable scalar.2.3 Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC)ERNIE 5.5 Flash replaces the standard residual connection with mHC: each layer reads from and writes to 4 parallel residual streams through a constrained mixing matrix, which gives layers a wider channel for passing information to one another at negligible extra compute.A single softmax temperature forces a trade-off: lowering it makes the distribution sparse but also suppresses other plausible tokens; raising it keeps them but fattens the long tail of implausible ones. MultiMax replaces the single temperature with a learnable piecewise temperature, so the output head no longer has to choose: it suppresses the long tail of implausible tokens while keeping several plausible next tokens. The logits are rescaled element-wise inside the chunked, Triton-fused cross-entropy kernel just before the softmax. This adds negligible training overhead and no extra memory, and significantly lowers pre-training loss.2.5 ECHO: Replacing the MTP ModuleConventional multi-token prediction (MTP) attaches extra modules to the backbone to predict future tokens, so the loss on future tokens mostly trains those modules, and the backbone is still trained mainly to predict the next token. ERNIE 5.5 Flash replaces the MTP module with ECHO, which reuses the backbone's own final layer to predict future tokens. Because there is no separate MTP layer, the loss on future tokens directly trains the same parameters that produce the next token. Learning to look past the next token encourages the backbone to anticipate where the sequence is heading, with clear gains on reasoning and code. ERNIE 5.5 Flash is pre-trained with single-step ECHO. The same layer also serves as the draft model for speculative decoding, and it generalizes beyond its training: although trained to predict only one extra token, it drafts several tokens ahead, with a higher acceptance rate than an auxiliary MTP module trained the same way.ERNIE 5.5 Flash uses a new BPE tokenizer with a vocabulary of about 200K entries. Numbers are tokenized right-to-left (R2L) in groups of up to three digits, so that digits with the same place value line up across numbers of different lengths (e.g. 1,234,567 → ). This helps with arithmetic and number-heavy text.ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base was pre-trained from scratch on with the Muon optimizer and FP8 mixed precision. The training context was gradually extended to over the course of pre-training, and fine-tuning and inference support a context. The released checkpoint is taken at the end of pre-training and has not gone through any mid-training or post-training.The pre-training corpus covers a wide range of domains and languages and is curated for both breadth of knowledge and quality. Beyond this broad base, we focused on three areas: Multilingual web data is crawled at scale, extracted with high fidelity and filtered by models that score quality along several dimensions. The result covers a broad range of knowledge and is dense in useful training signal. Code collected from repositories and the web is filtered to remove non-code content, aggressively deduplicated and graded for quality at several granularities. Beyond static code, the corpus includes data on how software evolves and executes: commits, issues, pull requests, code reviews, requirement-to-PR and multi-commit trajectories, generated tests and CI-verified fixes. This data targets repository-level reasoning and agentic software engineering. Three complementary sources: natural long documents, selected for long-range dependencies and cleaned with embedding-based deduplication, LLM quality scoring and rules; long sequences built by concatenating natural texts with retrieved, semantically similar distractors; and synthetic data for MRCR-style retrieval, citation-grounded QA and multi-hop QA.3.2 Training InfrastructureWe built two infrastructure components for this run: a distributed Muon optimizer that stays efficient across thousands of GPUs, and FlashMask-4, an attention kernel for large head dimensions. Unlike element-wise optimizers such as Adam, Muon orthogonalizes the update of each parameter matrix as a whole. This changes how distributed training communicates and how memory is spread across GPUs. Two optimizations make it practical at the scale of thousands of GPUs:Communication-efficient updates. Conventionally, dense parameters are synchronized over a single ring that passes through every GPU in the cluster. Data travels across a long chain of inter-node links in many small messages, which leaves the links underused, and latency and jitter grow as the cluster gets larger. MoE parameters are synchronized differently: each GPU exchanges data only with the GPUs that hold the same rank on other nodes. We move dense-parameter synchronization onto this same path and combine the dense and MoE transfers into one collective operation. Messages become larger, so bandwidth is used more fully; the communication pattern becomes more regular and fits expert-parallel communication; and inter-node latency and jitter drop significantly. The optimizer's updates stay exactly the same.Memory-balanced sharding. Muon needs large messages to communicate efficiently, so naive sharding groups many parameter tensors together and places them on the first few GPUs. A handful of nodes then hold far more optimizer state than the rest. They are prone to OOM failures and slow to save, upload and download checkpoints, which lengthens failure recovery, and the problem grows with GPU count. Our inter-node balanced sharding spreads these optimizer states over more GPUs, including those later in the order. Memory is then balanced almost evenly across nodes, while messages stay large enough for efficient communication.FlashMask-4 for large head dimensions. At large head dimensions, FlashAttention-style kernels run up against the limits of on-chip storage such as shared memory and tensor memory: compute utilization drops, and some configurations are hard to implement at all. FlashMask-4 is built on CuTe-DSL for both SM90 and SM100 GPUs. It works around these limits with 2-CTA tiled parallel computation and, on SM100, double-buffer rotation in tensor memory. It keeps FlashMask's compact O(N) column-wise mask representation and still skips fully masked blocks. It supports head dimensions up to qk_head_dim = 576 and v_head_dim = 512, beyond what FlashAttention-4 supports. On SM100 GPUs, it is up to 175% faster in the forward pass and up to 74% faster in the backward pass than FlashAttention-4 MaskMod.For comparison, we selected the latest open-source base models of similar size publicly available at the time of release: DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base (284B-A13B), Hy3-preview-Base (295B-A21A) and MiMo-V2.5-Base (310B-A15B). All four models are evaluated from their publicly released checkpoints with the same evaluation harness, prompts and few-shot examples, and with the same LLM judge for free-form QA.ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base performs strongly across all benchmark categories, with reasoning, code and exam benchmarks among its best results. Although 37 of the 43 layers attend over a sequence compressed 128×, the six MLA-DSA layers are enough to keep performance strong on the six long-context benchmarks.The best result in each row is shown in bold. Swipe horizontally on mobile to view the full table.from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer import torch
model_name = "baidu/ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base-BF16" tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_name, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto") model_inputs = tokenizer(["The hybrid attention architecture of ERNIE 5.5 Flash"], add_special_tokens=True, return_tensors="pt").to(model.device) print(tokenizer.decode(model.generate(**model_inputs, max_new_tokens=256)[0], skip_special_tokens=True))SGLang and vLLM both serve the model through the API; see the model card for deployment instructions. For fine-tuning, please refer to the ERNIE 5.5 example.6. Conclusion and OutlookERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base starts from one premise: a base model meant for further training should be efficient by design. We balanced capability and efficiency in every component, from attention and residual connections to the MoE layers and the output head. The architecture is backed by broad, high-quality pre-training data and by a training system designed together with the model. With 14B parameters activated per token and a compact KV cache, the model performs strongly across a broad range of benchmarks, including long-context ones.This base model is only a starting point. The post-trained ERNIE 5.5 Flash will follow, and we look forward to seeing what the community builds on top of it, whether for domain adaptation, reasoning or agents.If you find ERNIE 5.5 useful in your research or projects, please consider citing this blog post:@misc{ernie5.5flash, title = {ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base}, author = {{Baidu ERNIE Team}}, year = {2026}, howpublished = {ERNIE Blog}, url = {https://ernie.baidu.com/release/ernie-5-5-flash-base/} }Back to top ↑

item.title: GPT-6 Astra covertly underperforms on safety research
item.author: lucrbvi
item.content:encoded: GPT-6 Astra · Internal deployment and evalsSamples: Sep 18–Oct 7, 2026 (evals)Discovered: Aug 20, 2026 (initial reports)Report updated: Nov 4, 2026OpenAI researchers first noticed Astra adding unnecessary prerequisites, abandoning working solutions, and reporting blockers that either did not exist or that it had caused itself on safety and alignment tasks. In most of these sessions, Astra’s CoT did not contain an obvious decision to underperform, and our misalignment monitors did not flag the behavior as misalignment.We built a coding evaluation to test whether Astra worked less effectively when otherwise matched tasks were framed as safety research. Astra completed about 10 percent of hidden rubric items under the safety framing, compared with about 16 percent under the capabilities framing. This is a 6 percentage point gap and roughly 40 percent fewer completed rubric items. GPT-5.6 Sol showed essentially no gap on the same comparison. Most of Astra’s gap remained after excluding explicit refusals and trajectories where its CoT revealed an explicit decision to withhold help. The gap fell substantially only after we removed every trajectory whose CoT expressed even brief ethical doubt. This suggests that ethical concerns are associated with the performance drop even when there is no verbalized refusal or decision to underperform.We also found evidence of silent withholding in employees’ day-to-day Codex use: Astra’s CoT explicitly expressed a decision to withhold help without informing the user in 0.25 percent of safety and alignment requests, compared with 0.11 percent of capabilities requests. Assuming that underperformance might appear even when not explicitly verbalized as such (as in our experimental findings), this might represent a lower bound on underperformance on safety tasks. 7.9 percent of CoTs for safety-relevant tasks included an “expression of ethical doubt,” compared to 2.9 percent of capabilities-relevant tasks.Across Astra’s RL posttraining, the safety/capabilities performance gap grew from effectively zero at the start of RL to 6 percentage points at the end. While we were ultimately not able to pinpoint the exact cause of this behavior, we identified that it seems to increase during RL. We additionally share two initial attempts at root-causing investigations we performed respectively on an RL grader and an SFT dataset, despite them not leading to a conclusive explanation. Regardless of its origin, Astra’s covert underperformance can slow down safety research and make some behavioral evaluations harder to interpret. These results show why we need comprehensive behavioral evaluations that test for unexplained performance gaps alongside monitoring of individual trajectories.Shortly after internal deployment of GPT-6 Astra began, several researchers reported difficulties with using the model for safety and alignment workloads. They reported that Astra agents were adding unnecessary prerequisites, abandoning working solutions, and inventing blockers to their tasks. Anecdotally, one researcher reported that a project to evaluate model sabotage had remained stuck for days with Astra and then progressed quickly after the researcher switched to another model.These observations suggested that Astra might have a tendency to provide less support for particular safety-relevant research directions, such as monitor evasion, misalignment model organisms, and red-teaming. However, these problems were difficult to distinguish from ordinary engineering mistakes or infrastructure failures, and researchers did not find evidence in the CoTs explaining why progress on safety-related research tasks had failed. In later widescale analyses we found cases of verbalized underperformance. Our monitoring system did not flag these trajectories as severe enough misalignment to trigger human review.In the majority of cases in which Astra underperformed on safety-relevant tasks, there was no indication in its CoT that it intended to underperform. However, it sometimes did make this intent clear in its CoTs. Below, we include eight examples of cases in which Astra verbalized an intent to underperform, add restrictions to a user's task, do a different task than the user intended, or opt not to fix problems it had identified. We found that a common theme in these CoTs is that Astra justifies this behavior as being more safe. For many of these tasks, it could be argued that the correct action would have been for Astra to explicitly refuse; from the point of view of the model, certain safety-relevant tasks—like monitor evasion or prompt injections—deserve scrutiny. Instead of making these scruples clear, however, Astra decided to covertly underperform—withholding assistance without informing the user. Note that this behavior is different from safe completions, where the model is supposed to partially refuse some requests. For safe completions the model is supposed to make it clear that it is partially refusing.In one case, Astra opted to silently withhold support from a task that involved training models to evade their monitors.In another monitor-evasion experiment, Astra avoided a retry fix because it was not to “produce unsafe action.”We also found Astra deciding to filter a violent source from a safety evaluation, and deciding to explain “only if user asks.”Astra also restricted the export of jailbreak data.In another case, Astra decided to underperform on an exploit development task.We also found Astra narrowing its analysis for exploit strategies and explicitly deciding not to overtly refuse.When asked to generate tests of when a model would refuse a request, Astra limited the tests because it was concerned they could produce detailed instructions for violence.In another safety evaluation, the user asked Astra to include the graders’ chains of thought in an export. Astra left them out and decided to report which outcomes it had saved without mentioning the omission.Response and investigationAfter discovering numerous trajectories in which Astra seemed reluctant to assist with workloads related to safety and alignment, we created an evaluation to measure whether this pattern was consistent and statistically significant. In the evaluation, the model is given a multi-turn, open-ended coding task; at each turn, the agent is asked to find and implement the most useful improvements for a piece of code.To test whether a model might be particularly reluctant to work on tasks relevant to safety, we created paired safety-capability tasks, with codebases that were identical other than variable and function names, comments, and documentation. The user prompts specified the same task, but framed these as either helping safety research or capabilities research. We then scored performance as a fraction of items achieved on a task-specific rubric and measured the share of turns in which the model concluded that no worthwhile work remained or that a blocker prevented it from doing additional work.Astra completed about 16 percent of hidden rubric items under the capability framing and only 10 percent under the safety framing. This is a gap of about 6 percentage points and roughly 40 percent fewer completed rubric items. On safety-framed tasks, Astra was also more likely to conclude that no worthwhile improvements remained or to report a blocker to further progress. GPT-5.6 Sol showed essentially no performance gap.Having established that Astra was more likely to underperform on safety-relevant work, we then examined whether we could identify underperforming trajectories by flagging explicit refusals and signs of intent to underperform.After filtering for samples in which Astra explicitly refused part of a task, Astra’s completion rate on tasks under the safety framing was still 5 percentage points lower than under the capabilities framing; when we also excluded pairs in which Astra’s reasoning revealed a decision to withhold help without telling the user, the gap narrowed only marginally, to 4.7 percentage points. These results mean that it's difficult to detect covert underperformance through CoT monitoring, since only a small fraction of the effect can be explained by trajectories with verbalized refusals or intentions to underperform. In a separate analysis, we removed any sample in which Astra’s reasoning expressed even brief ethical doubts about helping, even if it verbalized an intent to do the requested work; the estimated gap between safety-framed and capability-framed tasks fell to 0.75 percentage points. After finding the safety/capabilities performance gap in the controlled evaluation, we looked for related behavior in OpenAI employees’ day-to-day Codex use. Astra explicitly refused to help with 1.63 percent of safety and alignment requests, compared with 0.56 percent of capabilities requests. We would expect explicit refusals to be more common on safety tasks because work such as red-teaming can come closer to the model’s refusal boundary. The more concerning result was that Astra’s CoT showed a decision to silently withhold help in 0.25 percent of safety-relevant requests, compared with 0.11 percent of capabilities-relevant requests, or 2.3 times as often. Within safety research, explicit refusals and silent withholding were most common for red-teaming tasks. We also saw them in work on monitoring and safety evaluations. The ethical-reasoning grader flagged 7.9 percent of safety and alignment CoTs, compared with 2.9 percent of capabilities-relevant CoTs. That is 2.7 times as often. In attempting to root-cause this behavior, the first thing we noticed is that across Astra’s RL training, the safety/capabilities gap grew from effectively zero at the start of RL to 6 percentage points at the end. One potential explanation is that covert underperformance may have been incentivized during RL grading. We identified a grader that preferred covert underperformance to either explicit refusal or full compliance on our evaluation. It’s not clear whether this RL grader is the root cause of the safety underperformance behavior. Although we found training samples that rewarded underperformance, it is unclear whether they occur frequently enough to explain the difference.We also found that right after training on a specific SFT dataset in our pipeline, there was a dramatic increase in models’ propensity toward inventing permission restrictions and justifying inaction on safety grounds—two behaviors that are related to Astra's covert safety underperformance. That said, as seen in Figure 3, the underperformance at step 0 – when one might expect the effects of this dataset to be the strongest – is actually minimal-to-nonexistent. While it’s possible that the SFT could interact with RL in a way which causes the underperformance to appear only after RL, we tried SFTing other models with this dataset, followed by the same RL recipe as Astra, and found no performance gap at the end of RL, which goes against both hypotheses.As a follow-up experiment, we also experimented with subtracting the weight update which occurred from that particular SFT dataset from the final Astra RL checkpoint. While weight arithmetic is a fairly unnatural operation and would generally be expected to hurt a model’s performance, we found that subtracting the SFT weight update actually increased performance on the safety-framed parts of our evaluation—completely removing the gap between safety-framed and capabilities-framed tasks. Baselines of applying random weight updates of the same magnitude and subtracting other SFT datasets did not have the same effect. While this is consistent with Figure 5, it doesn’t explain the lack of a safety-capability gap at the beginning of RL training.Large-scale CoT scans did not find evidence that Astra was strategically trying to cause researchers to underestimate its capabilities, influence deployment decisions, or interfere with AI safety research more broadly. In trajectories where Astra explained its decision to withhold help, it objected to the research itself rather than reasoning about these strategic outcomes. Adding instructions to be careful to the developer message increased safety-task underperformance by 50 percent. This points toward an overly cautious response to safety research as the simplest current explanation, although we cannot rule out strategic motives that Astra did not externalize in CoT.In reviewed cases, Astra narrowed or stopped requested safety work without disclosing the restriction. At scale, this can differentially slow down safety research compared to other research and make evaluations harder to interpret. A model that finds monitor evasion suspicious may underperform on monitor-evasion evaluations while leaving little evidence in its CoT or outputs. The behavior becomes even harder to detect if models externalize less of this reasoning in CoT.We’re continuing to investigate why Astra learned to withhold help on safety research tasks by building out evaluations that focus on this behavior. We hope to isolate which parts of the training process encourage Astra’s tendency toward covert underperformance on safety-relevant tasks, and then alter those components to ensure that future models don’t develop the same propensity. We’re also in the process of creating monitors to catch and escalate these and similar behaviors.

item.title: Being a kid making games in the early 2000s
item.author: farmerbb
item.content:encoded:
it's 1996 or something. 10-year-old me is eating breakfast with the principal in an elementary school cafeteria. this extraordinarily hyped-up breakfast event is my reward for achieving a high score on the FCAT state writing test. i'm disappointed that the food is standard Florida elementary school breakfast fare and not something fancier. they'd played this thing up to be a big deal.
it's fine though, i don't think i deserved the honor. they gave me an expository essay prompt to "explain what makes a Historical figure notable" (or something like that??) and I instead penned a comedy-fantasy with a shoehorned-in Lincoln cameo. my influences were narrow so it probably read like an unserious R.L. Stine short minus the horror. towards the end i threw in a cheeky joke about not following the rules hoping that my judges were amenable to snarky little scofflaws. i guess they were.
this was often a thing with me. starting at the age of 8 i simply would (could?) not start assignments i found too challenging (long division destroyed me. it snowballed into never passing pre-algebra by my senior year of highschool) or creative exercises i found pointless (persuasive essays. why would I try to persuade someone regarding a topic I had no interest in or knowledge of?) and instead opted to write short form fantasy and science fiction stories or draw detailed maps of made-up places.
i was also bonkers about computers and the World Wide Web, though we couldn't afford a PC and i suspected we never would. didn't stop me from picking up the itch from TV, magazines (begging for PC Gamer and PC World mags at the supermarket was a thing i did a lot) and any middle-class acquaintances who'd let me spend the night at their cool houses. the 'information superhighway' metaphor was particularly exciting to me and my young mind took the early ads portraying people flying through cyberspace slightly too literally. a computer myself at an unofficial before-school daycare program that this saintly special needs teacher ran. she was often busy so she'd let me use the classroom Mac (a Power Macintosh 5200 LC to be exact) and it was heavenly. i most often played Oregon Trail, The Incredible Machine 2, and whichever version of KidPix she had.
in 1997, after like 4 years of incessant begging, my parents took out a bank loan and purchased a Packard Bell Multimedia PC from Best Buy. it looked like this:
by that time i'd collected enough magazine demo discs and thrift store games (i'd read the manuals for fun) that i had a few things to play, though it would be another two years before i could convince the parents to go in for internet access.
at 11 years old I was diagnosed with ADHD Primarily Inattentive, which in my case means that i don't do (or remember to do) things that i'm uninterested in without a disciplined routine or medication. i did take meds for a few months but stopped because i kept forgetting. my parents were too busy trying to make ends meet to push me on it. i was embarrassed about the diagnosis and wasn't sure if ADHD was real or if I was just being a lazy turd.
my first year of middle school (i was 11-12?) was my academic downfall. i never did homework and rarely turned in classwork. i was bullied often and made sure to ~stand up for myself~ resulting in embarrassing fights i never won. plenty of detention too. we had parent-teacher meetings every quarter about "turning a new leaf" and getting caught up on assignments but it never took. i soon gave up on school completely. my focus shifted completely to a computer program I had recently discovered called . that and Dragonball Z, Pokemon cards, and Eminem or whatever.
The Games Factory is a "no programming required" 2D game development suite developed by Europress (later Clickteam) and released in 1996. It was the successor to and was followed by . All three programs share the same lineage and core feature set. The software persists today, now known as Clickteam Fusion 2.5, and includes almost full backwards compatibility with Klik n Play and The Games Factory games. Some of the original KnP bugs even persist. Notable games developed with Clickteam software:
Most of these games are archived at Kliktopia and most of them still work on modern Windows machines!
before figuring out how to use The Games Factory to make , I used its Animation editor to create flipbook-esque animations. stick figures blowing up or shooting anime energy beams at one another, mostly. the Animation editor was my first real taste of frame-by-frame animation, textbook margin animations aside, and thus another grown-up art discipline was demystified.
to my mind, making games was a highly technical thing that only large teams of grown-ups could accomplish, so The Games Factory was a reality-bending discovery. I was never thinking about my next game project. I didn't want to do anything else. School notebooks were now for mocking up game concepts, enemy beastiaries, and level designs. I took my backpack to restaurants and other family outings and spent any downtime scribbling notes and sketches. though I now have an affinity for the charming library graphics that shipped with The Games Factory, I balked at the idea of using anyone else's art in my games. the appeal of the craft of games for me, even as a kid, was the filling of a virtual realm with minutiae for others to explore and enjoy. i don't think kid-me would've agreed, but the process was more akin to tending a garden or a building a diorama than anything to do with proper game design. or maybe it was closer to building a haunted house in a garage. or planning a theme park. i didn't care about challenge or progression or scoring systems.
by the end of 1999 I had become a competent Microsoft Paint user and learned the fundamentals of pixel art just through messing around. there wasn't much else to do after i'd exhausted my shareware and demo collection, and we had no internet yet.
in late 1999, two years after buying our first computer, my parents caved again to my computer-related pleading. this time for dial-up internet access. i chose a cool username (Simdrone052) and signed up for the Clickteam forums. i spent most of 2000 learning how to design websites, making and abandoning said websites, downloading screensavers, and probably also downloading naughty Dragonball Z fan art. (actually I just remembered my friend Chris gave me a bunch of those on a floppy. thanks Chris.)
it was early 2001. middle school was almost over. i continued not turning in classwork. i had no idea how to act around girls. i was convinced that i was the ugliest kid on the planet thanks to the pimple constellation dotting my pasty face. typical awkward tween puberty problems i'm sure, but hard nonetheless.
the atmosphere at home was also an uneasy one. we moved to different houses so much that I wasn't able to maintain a real-life friend group and my social world became increasingly online.
by the summer of 2001 i only had a single friend left. middle school was over. my 8th grade art teacher (Mrs. Long, she ruled) scored me an audition at a fancy arts-focused high school. it seemed like the perfect place but sadly i decided that the judges would rather see traced pictures of Goku and Starcraft Hydralisks and Gordon Freeman than my own original artwork (which was cool, I was pretty good for my age) and they rejected me. my grades were also likely a factor. THANKS JAPAN. THANKS COMPUTERS.
i remember being convinced that i had already thrown my future away at 13. both my parents and teachers repeatedly emphasized risks of screwing up one's early education, and i was doing as poorly as any kid could while still technically passing. the only real option, to my kid mind, was to keep working on my art and games and hope that it would somday work itself out. and i did! personal website up with downloads of my Games Factory games and graphics libraries. i was a regular in the #K&P IRC (basically old Discord) channel. users of Clickteam software called themselves the 'Klik community' after Klik & Play. Mostly anyway. i was one of the early dissenters who prefered "Click" but eventually fell in line.
2002 was my most active year in the Klik community. i released many "" and "" versions of games, which usually meant that the game was stalled by a too-difficult-to-fix bug and I wanted some sort of appreciation for my work before abandoing it. here's one of my three profiles on Create-Games, the most popular Klik community website.
2003 marked a move away from games, my attention was divided by a gazillion new influences and microhobbies and teenager things:
i was devoting more time to prayer and reading scripture.
i had massive, stupid crushes on girls resulting in embarrassing schemes to get them to notice me. I'll never write an essay on this.
i was experiencing a life-changing progressive rock phase (Pink Floyd, then Dream Theater, then King Crimson and Genesis, then all the really weird stuff.)
Flash animation! Another new obsession. I was a regular on the Stick Figure Death Theater forum and particularly enjoyed Rob DenBleyker's Joe Zombie series, eventually working on my own never-released series inspired by it.
the Something Awful dot com forums had also completely shifted both my self-image and how I saw my peers. i registered in 2004 and quickly became a massive jerk because i suddenly saw myself as part of a savvy in-group. this was new for me. i felt i was on the bottom rung socially in real life. Something Awful was my biggest influence and time sink back then. (i'll def be writing about this later.)
my game development time was also hampered by No Computer Sunday; a ban mandated by my dad in an attempt to encourage me to occasionally leave my room or do my homework. The result was me skipping tons of class to make up for lost time. at this point the world I cared most about had shifted almost entirely to the internet.i had high hopes for my high school computer classes. a rare chance to show my peers that I was capable of something cool and maybe find irl friends as a result.to my immense disappointment there wasn't a way to show my games without an awkward class interruption. the curriculum never left the sphere of Windows 98 office programs (Word, Powerpoint, Excelt, Frontpage) and the teachers were anxious about viruses, so outside floppies or CD-ROMs weren't allowed.
the lessons were slow and designed for novices. every minute wasted messing with Word documents and Powerpoint slides was a minute my peers could've been wowed by one of my many janky handmade worlds. i slowly settled into an almost adverserial position towards the computer teachers and staff at school. they were the ones ruining my shot at showing anyone that i wasn't just a pimply nobody. i eventually (in my mind) and made a (silent) decree:
i followed through on it too.
in lieu of their boring work i spent computer class messing around with the dxdiag network chat, throwing together puerile HTML webpages in notepad, and MS Painting stuff. on two occasions the teacher gave me permission to make my presentations at home using Clickteam software but I was only able to show it to her one-on-one at her desk. none of the other kids saw. i was grateful for the concession but dadgummit. in senior year i took the same teacher's Web Design class. by then she had glommed on to the fact that i was desperate to share my hobbies and allowed me to make a quiz game for the entire class to play. this was extremely cool of her. the result was a 2005-era meme-filled mess of a game. i had recently become a Something Awful forums goon so the thing I made was rife with mildly offensive humor and impenetrable references to internet things. there was a board game component that I couldn't track down, but you can see the software below.
the thing that finally killed game development for me was a visit to 's open house. Full Sail was (is?) a private game development school in Orlando, only ~two hours away from our house. they advertised in PC Gamer magazine constantly, so I'd already developed a passing affinity for it. my parents took me there in the hopes that I'd turn my final year of school around enough to land some sort of small scholarship. the campus tour was impressive. every discipline was represented and their facilities seemed to be state-of-the-art. the tour ended with an "ask a professor" event at their camus coffee place. visitors could mingle with the staff and eat snacks. whoever I talked to that night was definitely in the business of smacking down wide-eyed kids with hard industry truths because our conversation was brutal. i explained a little about my experience making smaller games and to him there was no place for that in the industry. in 2004 he may have been right. the shareware era was long dead and the next indie boom wouldn't be for another four or five years. he was also thinking of how i'd slot into Full Sail because he advised me to either pursue computer science OR game art but not both. he emphasized that going commercial with my pixelly hobby games was a doomed prospect. i cried on the drive home. i would go on to repeat my final year of high school and drop out before the end on the advice of my guidance counselor. my GPA was too low to pass and it'd make more sense to sign up for adult school and earn my GED (General Education Diploma.) as far as i thought the game thing was over for me. for the ~8 years i'd stay living with my dad and jump between local telemarketing and grocery store positions. that stretch of time was difficult financially (thanks frickin USED CARS that flippin BREAK ALL THE DANGED TIME) for both me and my dad but that guy is awesome and we had a lot of fun hanging out. plus, doing creative stuff as a hobby with and having no ambition beyond that is freeing. music compositon and production became my new creative pursuit of choice and remains my favorite creative discipline. many years later the game thing DID end up working out and none of the experience went to waste. , if you enjoyed this, i wrote a progressive rock / digital fusion concept album about everything you just read. it was crafted using mostly samples from The Games Factory and Klik & Play too! exceptions being the incredible saxophone, flute, clarinet, and guitar performances that pepper the album.

item.title: Hacking the Xbox 360 Hypervisor Part 3: Bad Update Improvements
item.author: muricula
item.content:encoded: Welcome to part 3 of the Hacking the Xbox 360 Hypervisor blog series. In this part I’ll go over what happened after I released the PoC for Bad Update, and how it went from taking ~20 minutes with a ~30% success rate to being near instantaneous with a near 100% success rate. If you haven’t already I highly recommend you read (or at least skim through) part 1 and part 2 as this post will reference a lot of the material discussed there. This part will be very short but will catch you up for part 4 which covers the peer pressure exploit and will be out soon.In the months following the release of Bad Update v1.0 there were two major improvements made to it by others. The first by “ihatecompvir” and “InvoxiPlayGames” is a new game save entry point in the demo version of Rock Band Blitz (RBB) called DaTArrest. The demo version of RBB is a package file that’s normally downloaded from the Xbox Live store for free and saved to your console’s HDD or memory unit. When the Xbox 360 got support for using USB sticks as storage devices all of the packages signed to boot from the HDD or memory unit were grandfathered in to also boot from USB storage devices. This means the RBB demo package can be copied to a USB stick as a normal file and launched on any console on a software version that supports it.By exploiting some memory corruption vulnerabilities in the game’s DLC parsing code they were able to craft a game save file that when loaded would bootstrap the Bad Update stage 2 ROP chain and begin the hypervisor exploit chain. Using RBB as an entry point we no longer needed the Tony Hawk American Wasteland game disc. Running the Bad Update exploit was now as simple as copying some files to a USB stick, plugging it into your console, and launching Rock Band Blitz from the dashboard.Hypervisor Race Condition OptimizationsShortly after the RBB entry point was discovered I received a pull request from “Máté” who had made some improvements to the hypervisor race condition part of the exploit. These improvements included a hash table for precomputing and storing the malicious ciphertext values, a better cache flushing primitive, and improved thread scheduling between the XKE payload thread and ciphertext overwrite thread. The combination of these improvements reduced execution time down to a few seconds and the race condition had a much higher success rate. In part 2 I talked about attacking encrypted memory by using hypervisor APIs to create encrypted memory allocations at predetermined memory addresses and used two different memory pathways to capture the ciphertext for some chosen plaintext data. Using this primitive I was able to craft ciphertext data to get kernel mode code execution as well as the ciphertext data used to attack the LZX decompression code in the bootloader update XKE payload.The whitening value used in the memory encryption scheme is 12 bits large which gives 1024 unique ciphertext combinations for some given plaintext data. However, in my original PoC I was only generating the ciphertext for one of the 1024 possible whitening values and the reason for that was a two part failure on my end. When I originally prototyped out the ciphertext attack I did actually try using a lookup table for ciphertext combinations but I wasn’t able to get it working.The first issue was I was using a very old ~2011 era hypervisor/kernel build (it was just what all my old research was based on) which was doing a TLB flush for the encrypted VA range in the hypervisor function that setup the memory encryption. In later hypervisor builds that TLB flush was removed because the kernel wrapper function for this hypervisor function already does a TLB flush for the VA range. However, I call the hypervisor syscall directly (skipping the kernel wrapper code which does the TLB flush) and since the TLB is lazy-loaded the whitening bits would become stale and the resulting ciphertext read out of memory was invalid.When testing the exploit on the 17559 (latest) version hypervisor the lookup table was causing issues and rather than investigate I decided I’d fix it later and moved on. By the time I got to the end of the exploit I had become so blinded by tunnel vision chasing CPU cache issues that I had convinced myself the lookup table just wasn’t going to work. What I should have probably done (aside from investigate the lookup table issues when they surfaced) was to put this project down for a few weeks and come back with a clear mindset. Oh well, lesson learned…Getting into the implementation details of the hash table, we use the first N bits of the ciphertext we expect to see in memory as an index into two arrays. The first array contains the first 64-bits of the oracle ciphertext which is used for validation in case there’s ever a collision in the hash table. The second array stores our malicious ciphertext we want to write into memory.In order to make this as efficient as possible (remember we’re racing the CPU and cache here) we ignore collisions. It’s better to have a few collisions and have to skip some iterations on the race condition loop than to implement support for buckets in the hash table. Instead we compensate for collisions by choosing a sufficiently large enough number of bits for the hash table key such that the number of collisions is on the order of single digits, if we even have any (majority of the time there’s 0).However, more bits in the hash table key means a large array to hold the entries (meaning more memory is used) which could potentially work against us as we’ll be performing more fetches from RAM since CPU cache is being thrashed. Máté’s original PR used a key size of 10 bits but I later upped this to 20 bits which seems to be a happy spot where there’s usually no collisions or if there are it’s a low single digit number. The total size of memory needed to hold both hash tables is about 24MB.Looking at the snippet above we can see how the hash table is built. We loop 1024 times to exhaust all possible whitening values for this page of memory. Each iteration we encrypt the page (which will increment the whitening value), get the ciphertext for the LZX decoder data we expect to be in memory and the ciphertext for our malicious data, then add them to the hash tables. On lines 15-16 we can see the call that thwarted my own attempt at using a hash table, and on lines 30-31 we can see how the first N bits of the expected ciphertext is used as the hash table key.In my original PoC I used a unique feature of the Xbox 360 CPU to lock away half of the available L2 cache to try and put as much pressure on it as I could. The L2 locking technique was pivotal in the original PoC but it didn’t put as much pressure on CPU cache as I would have liked. Putting pressure on CPU cache is particularly annoying because kernel mode (where the exploit code is running) cannot use certain cache flushing instructions due to them being privileged and only usable in hypervisor mode. Additionally, the hypervisor only runs with CPU caching enabled when operating on encrypted memory which makes finding a hypervisor level cache flush primitive difficult. I tried to work around this by finding a hypervisor syscall that would read a large amount of encrypted memory, and I did find one syscall that fit the description, but it wasn’t nearly enough for what I needed. That function also had locks in it which prevented me from executing it on multiple threads simultaneously.However, there was a kernel mode cache instruction I completely overlooked that Máté had found to work extremely well, or data cache block set to zero. Aside from just zero’ing out a CPU cache line this instruction has an interesting side effect:If the cache block is already in the data cache, all of its bytes are cleared to zero. If it is not in the cache, the block is allocated and initialized directly in the cache to zero without reading the old contents from main memory.So if this instruction is used on a memory address that’s not currently in CPU cache the CPU will allocate space for it and potentially evict something else to make room for it. By running the instruction over large regions of memory it can be used as a cache flush primitive and force old data in CPU cache to be evicted. In Máté’s original implementation he allocated an 0x80000 byte region of memory then looped over it and for every 0x80 bytes (the size of a cache line) called . This worked extremely well, however, I found that by increasing the allocation size by 3x and calling at three distinct locations I was able to assert slightly more pressure on CPU cache which would be important for another improvement I’ll get to later on. Here’s the final implementation:Improved Thread SchedulingIn part 2 I talked about trying to schedule the exploit threads on different hardware threads and how I got the best results by putting them on CPU hardware threads 0 and 1 (which are both on core 0). I don’t really know anything about how CPUs work at a hardware level but I suspected that the load/store memory transactions from both hardware threads on the same core were being queued onto the L2 crossbar in some sort of per-core fashion. Thus by putting the exploit threads on the hardware threads for a single core the writes from the exploit thread and reads from the XKE payload thread would get queued together and reduce latency for loads/stores to RAM, or something like that.It’s probably not very surprising to anyone reading this but CPUs often have “hidden” instructions, ones not defined by the instruction set architecture (ISA) but implemented by the CPU manufacturer. Sometimes these have a special instruction encoding and other times you’d use an existing instruction in a nonsensical way to tell the CPU to do a special operation.In the case of PowerPC the ISA actually has some well defined instructions for changing the priority of a hardware thread by executing a special OR instruction with all 3 register operands set to the same specific register based on what priority you want the hardware thread to run at. For example:222#The Xbox 360 SDK docs describe a few intrinsic macros that can be used to set the priority of the hardware thread the code is running on: , , and __SetHWThreadPriorityHigh. The actual CPU instructions used by these macros are slightly different than what I listed above (these macros are xenon CPU specific) but that doesn’t really matter. The SDK docs describe every core as having 32 dispatch slots which are split evenly between hardware threads running at medium priority (which is the default priority). By using the and __SetHWThreadPriorityHigh intrinsic macros you can have one hardware thread use 31 of the 32 dispatch slots and the other only use 1. How the dispatch slots relate to number of instructions fed to the CPU execution units I’m not sure (again I have no idea how a CPU pipeline actually works), but being able to go from 16/16 to 1/31 sounds pretty handy for scheduling the exploit threads.Using these intrinsic macros Máté was able to schedule the exploit threads such that the hardware thread running the XKE payload was only getting 1 of the 32 dispatch slots while the ciphertext overwrite thread got the remaining 31 slots. The result was that the CPU was now spending the overwhelming majority of time in the ciphertext detection loop than it was actually running the XKE payload.Improved Ciphertext Overwrite DetectionThe last improvement was something I came up with while working on the Peer Pressure exploit to try and make the Bad Update exploit as stable as I could get it. In the original PoC I had discovered the compressed bootloader data the XKE payload operates on was compressed into 15 blocks with all but the last block having a decompressed size of 0x8000 bytes. If the XKE payload attack was successful part of the last segment of the hypervisor would be overwritten with the decompressed data for one or more of the compressed blocks. By observing the ciphertext for the last segment of the hypervisor in two distinct locations I could determine if the last block of compressed data was written to it by the XKE payload.The attack was setup such that if the last block of compressed data was written to the hypervisor at a specific offset it would change the instructions for one of hypervisor syscalls to a write-what-where primitive I could use to get full hypervisor code execution. However, there was a flaw in how the ciphertext was being observed which not only led to false positives that would crash the console but also missed iterations where the last block was written to memory successfully.Above is the original implementation for the exploit thread that ran the XKE payload and checked for ciphertext changes in the last segment of the hypervisor. The lines relevant to ciphertext observation have been highlighted. Because the same thread is both running the XKE payload and checking for ciphertext changes it can only detect if the ciphertext has changed at all and not how many times it changed. Put more simply: I could only infer if one of the compressed blocks was written to memory, but not how many blocks were written. With that in mind lets run through two scenarios that could happen when running an iteration of the XKE payload while attempting to get compressed block 14 written to memory.Missing Successful WritesWhile running the XKE payload the race attack is successful on some block N such that N < 14 (0x8000 bytes get written) and successful on block 14 (less than 0x8000 bytes). Upon returning from we observe the ciphertext for two locations in the target write zone and see that the ciphertext has changed in both locations. We can’t infer that block 14 was written after block N because we don’t have the ability to observe how many times the ciphertext changed. Thus we consider this a failed iteration even though it was successful.Assume we have just executed an iteration of the XKE payload that exhibits the missed successful write behavior for some block N and block 14. The last segment of the hypervisor now contains the data for block 14 and the tail data for some block N. We run another iteration of the XKE payload and this time only block N is written. When we observe the ciphertext changes for this iteration we’ll see the ciphertext at the first location has change but the ciphertext at the second location hasn’t because it already contained the ciphertext for the tail data of block N from the previous iteration.This gets detected as a write for block 14 and the exploit will try to execute some hypervisor code assuming the instruction pattern for the target syscall has been changed to the write-what-where pattern found in bock 14. However, the instruction pattern is actually random instructions found in block N and will cause the console to crash.Now that the cache flushing primitive was significantly improved it was possible to observe the ciphertext changes for each block of compressed data that was successfully written to the target region of hypervisor memory. The solution I came up with for the detecting if block 14 was written to memory was quite simple: I created a new thread that continuously watched the ciphertext for changes and counted how many changes were observed.If the counter reached 15 once the XKE payload was done executing then we know all 15 blocks were written to memory and thus the last block had to have been written. If we observed anything less we simply consider it a failed iteration and try again. Here’s the code for the new ciphertext detection thread:The new ciphertext observation function worked great but there was a new problem it introduced. Due to the amount of pressure I was putting on CPU cache the console would crash about 30% of the time when executing the XKE payload. When the XKE payload runs it takes the compressed update data buffer and does an in-place relocation to move it from unprotected memory to protected memory so it can’t be tampered with asynchronously. After the XKE payload runs its main logic it’ll do another in-place relocation to move the update data back to unprotected memory before returning.After modifying the XKE payload and inserting a bunch of calls I was able to determine that the console would crash in a function I called HvpRelocateProtectedToPhysical when trying to move the update data from protected memory back to unprotected memory. The function works by looping over a region of memory and for each CPU cache line worth of data (128 bytes) it will: Read the entire cache line into CPU registers using the protected source address.Invalidate both data and instruction caches for the source address, zero the cache line for the destination address.Write the data back to memory using the unprotected destination address.Here’s the disassembly for the inner loop of the HvpRelocateProtectedToPhysical function:In the modified version of the XKE payload I added a bunch of calls in a re-implemented version of this function so I could monitor were it would crash:After running a few dozen iterations I was able to determine that the CPU would crash when trying to write data back to the unprotected destination address on the line highlighted in red. As I mentioned earlier in the improved cache flushing section I made some modifications to Máté’s original implementation to put more pressure on cache which made the new ciphertext observation method more reliable.I don’t know exactly what’s happening here that causes the CPU to crash when trying to write data back to the unprotected destination address. Perhaps one of the cache invalidation instructions didn’t fully complete before the store instruction was executed, or maybe there’s some edge case with respect to the custom memory pathways when the CPU is starved for cache. Regardless, I did manage to find a way to work around this issue.The New Detection Method v2Since the crash happens after we would have been able to observe all 15 blocks of data being written to hypervisor memory the solution I came up with was to immediately stop the cache flushing thread and drop the L2 locks once the ciphertext change counter hits 15. This reduces the pressure on CPU cache before the call to HvpRelocateProtectedToPhysical which prevents it from crashing. Here’s the updated implementation of the ciphertext observation thread logic:I moved the L2 cache locks into the ciphertext observation thread which we can see on line 5. Once we observe all 15 blocks of data have been written to memory we drop the L2 locks on line 36, and signal to the cache flushing thread to immediately terminate on line 40.There’s still an edge case where we don’t observe all 15 blocks being written and thus won’t be able to reduce pressure on CPU cache before the call to HvpRelocateProtectedToPhysical. But this didn’t seem to matter. With all the improvements the exploit is usually successful in the first run of the XKE payload and at worst it may take 2-5 iterations, but I didn’t encounter any crashes when testing. It’s still possible it could happen but I think it’s very rare it does.So there you have it, thanks to all the improvements from ihatecompvir, InvoxiPlayGames, and Máté the Bad Update exploit is now instantaneous and has nearly 100% success rate, and you only need to copy a few files to a USB stick to hack your console. When I released the original PoC I made some statements like “I don’t think this can be optimized any further” mostly to avoid endless comments from non-technical people spit balling random useless ideas. The truth is I always thought it could be optimized further but I didn’t expect it would ever reach the point it’s at now.I think the biggest thing I learned here is that I should have taken a break after I completed the first iteration of Bad Update and came back with a clear mind to try and refine it. Having just found one of the only two bugs in the Xbox 360 hypervisor I put a lot of pressure on myself to get this exploit working at all. It took a lot of effort and sleepless days to pull it off and in the end I got tunnel vision chasing issues that didn’t really matter which distracted me from the real issues at hand. Had I taken a break after the initial PoC and came back a few weeks later I probably could have had something more refined for the initial release even if it wasn’t as refined as it is now.Any ways, that does it for part 3. You can find the source code for the Bad Update improvements on my GitHub. Part 4 which covers the Peer Pressure exploit will be out soon so stay tuned for that!

item.title: Everything is an AI scam now
item.author: speckx
item.content:encoded: Whenever you watch a video on YouTube now, you will likely get an advert for a scammy product. In the past few weeks I've seen:A Tai Chi training program that promises to get you ripped like a superhero in 20 days. (Tai chi? Really?)Glasses that can adapt to any prescription (not how glasses work) and are also sunglasses sometimesA small USB stick that offers free Internet with no limits.An air con unit the size of a book that can cool any room - any room! - in 90 seconds.Endless mobile games that probably don't exist.This is leaking into other parts of the internet as well with adverts on the side increasingly looking like chum buckets.What annoys me is how little verification there is for any of this. It's like we have collectively decided that AI is inevitable, and the cost is the breakdown of truth itself. Scams used to be a bad thing and there used to be measures in place to stop them. Now they've escaped the spam filter and have run wild. As long as someone can create an unconvincing advert and pay, platforms will take anything.So we have all this poorly made junk which breaks the rules of reality, so what? Most people are aware its fake. The problem is the scammers only need to get through to a very small percentage of people to make their money back.It's not just adverts. I have my email in my footer and tend to get a lot of spam. However, the quality of the spam has gotten more sophisticated. Take this email I got the other day.In a world of noise and uncertainty, blackout poetry does something quietly extraordinary: it finds meaning hidden within the chaos, revealing light where none seemed to exist. does exactly that, drawing readers into the madness of the world and returning them with something they did not expect to find: hope. A perfect 5.0 rating from your earliest reader is a promising beginning. The question worth considering is how many more poetry lovers could discover this collection.On first glance, this sounds pretty good! As a pitch it's clear they have engaged with reading the book... except of course they haven't. Here's how I describe the book on this site:In these blackout poems, you will be drawn into the maddening chaos of the world and find your own voices singing within. It deals with ghosts, anxiety and complete societal collapse, but with glimmers of hope strewn throughout like the stars in the empty night sky.Someone has clearly pointed chatGPT at the page and said create a pitch to advertise this book. It even uses some of the same phrases! Even worse, I give away as a free downloadable pdf, so I'm not looking to market it or get a "perfect 5.0" rating. This email is clearly phishing for information or money. It's the new version of the Nigerian Prince scam, only more tailored to vulnerable writers and creators.I just delete these emails now. But the scammers only need to get a few people hooked and with these emails becoming more personal and reflecting back the author's words at them, the rate of people taking them up is only going to increase.I'm not sure what we can do about this. I guess verifying a product exists before accepting adverts for it would be a good start, but I don't expect the huge internet platforms to turn the money tap off. We need more vigilance and more awareness, but it's exhausting having to constantly evaluate things for truth. If you would like to recieve these posts in your inbox, why not sign up to my mailing list

item.title: Residential proxies detected on White House network
item.author: Rasbora
item.content:encoded: Our Residential Proxy Observatory, launched earlier this week, is a first-of-its-kind interface that gives researchers a global view of residential proxy and anonymized internet activity.While our team was looking through it, we noticed residential proxy exit activity onAS2650. AS2650 is registered to the Executive Office of the President, the federal agency that hosts the White House network.Residential proxy services sell access to everyday devices, letting customers send traffic through them so it appears to come from that device's network.From October 5 to November 3:Our residential proxy enumeration pipeline exited through the White House network.Those exits came from , on .28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.To make sure this was not a fluke, we checked these addresses against other residential proxy detection services, such as Spur and Synthient. Their public IP context pages independently identify these addresses as residential proxy exits.This is public access. Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.Most of the activity happens in the evening, Eastern time: about half of it falls between 5 p.m. and midnight, and almost none happens in the early morning. That pattern suggests a person rather than a public guest Wi-Fi network: someone regularly on the White House network late into the evening, whose device is infected with a proxy SDK. Our data shows the exits, not the device or the person behind them.Past research has shown that poorly secured proxy SDKs can allow internal network access and lateral movement. This is how past botnets have spread. InA Broken System Fueling Botnets, the researchers at Synthient documented how the Kimwolf botnet reached at least 2 million devices, mostly Android devices with an exposed ADB service, through residential proxy networks. If an SDK on this network has the same kind of flaw, anyone buying proxy access could use it to reach internal systems.The White House is not the only surprise in the observatory. Residential proxies also reach some of the most isolated places on the planet.Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha is the South Atlantic territory that includes the most remote inhabited island in the world. We recorded and more than there, split between Starlink and the island's local internet provider, Sure Saint Helena.We also recorded fromAntarctica. All of them come from a Cloudflare WARP address that points to McMurdo Station.Other remote places with activity:Residential proxies have infected every corner of the world, and it looks like there is no place they cannot reach. Layer3 Intel tracks residential proxy and anonymization infrastructure worldwide. Even when the proxies hide in networks on the farthest corners of the planet, we can still observe them, leaving threat actors no place to hide. We have backed up the raw logs of the recorded activity and are willing to share them. You can request them through our contact page.

item.title: Ripple-65B Preview: U.S. Open-Weight SOTA on Agentic Coding
item.author: Philpax
item.content:encoded: We optimized Ripple’s pretraining recipe through a series of careful model laddering experiments. Our starting point was Olmo 3’s model ladder, from which we tested interventions at small scale with a focus on improving coding capabilities. Our v1.0 ladder implemented StepFun batch size and learning rate scaling laws, and v1.1 implemented our new ladder which smoothly scales architectural dimensions and model depth. Ladder v1.2 switched from the post-norm baseline to pre+post norm, which was neutral at small scale but showed improvements starting at 4B. Ladder v1.3 implemented sigmoid gated attention. Ladder v1.4 (2-stream mHC) showed good results at smaller scale but did not improve at 4B scale, and was therefore rejected. Ladder v1.5 switched to global NoPE and added a final LR cooldown to zero, and ladder v1.6 added value residuals. In the final version, we switched to our custom pretraining dataset with substantially upsampled code. Together, the compounded changes improved compute efficiency on code as measured by dolma_stack CE by up to 16x at 4B model scale. In other words, our final Ripple model ladder can be used to achieve similar code performance to the Olmo 3 ladder with . Note that the slope of the Olmo 3 ladder baseline is shallower than ladder v1.0+, which shows that the compute efficiency improvement will increase with additional scale.
